PROPOSED DESIGN INTERVENTION: Integrate nanoscale ZrO₂ particles into the existing glass-ceramic seal to enhance densification through constrained sintering. This modification targets the seal's structural integrity against thermal cycling fatigue while maintaining ionic insulation. The seal remains a glass-ceramic ionic insulator; no electronic conductors are introduced.

MECHANISM: Nanoscale ZrO₂ particles facilitate constrained sintering densification, which suppresses microcrack initiation at the cathode-electrolyte interface and within the seal. By reducing porosity and stabilizing the glass-ceramic matrix against thermal shock, the seal maintains gas tightness. Note: ZrO₂ CTE is comparable to or higher than typical glass phases; the benefit is densification-driven mechanical strength, not CTE reduction.

DEPARTURE FROM STANDARD: Standard approach adds bulk glass or changes seal chemistry for CTE matching. This design disperses nanoscale ZrO₂ to leverage sintering constraints for durability under rapid cycling without changing the seal's primary ionic insulation role.

LABELED PARAMETERS:
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Seal intergranular glass phase fraction = 0.15 (User Constraint; maintains specified composition)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: ZrO₂ particle size = 50-100 nm (Design choice to ensure effective sintering constraint without grain boundary blocking)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: ZrO₂ volume fraction = 5 vol% (Design choice to minimize mass increase and maintain sealability)
ASSUMPTION PARAMETER: Target seal leakage = <1% of fuel flow (User Constraint; required for OCV retention)

FALSIFICATION TEST: Expose n = 5 independent seal-cathode-electrolyte test cells to 500 thermal cycles from 25°C to 800°C at 5°C/min. Test duration: 30 days. Pass criterion: Open-circuit voltage remains >1.0 V and seal leakage stays below 1% of fuel flow after the 500th cycle, with total stack mass increase ≤2%.
